lead.headline: Myanmar jet bombs busy Rakhine market, killing dozens of civilians
lead.dek: A military air strike near the main wholesale market in Kyauktaw, in rebel-held Rakhine state, killed at least 33 people, a toll that later rose to 49.
body: A Myanmar military fighter jet dropped two bombs near the market in Kyauktaw, a town in northern Rakhine state, at around midday on Monday 28 September, according to the Arakan Army, the ethnic armed group that controls the area. Vendors, shoppers and passers-by were among the victims. The first count put the dead at 33 with 36 wounded, and the rebels warned the figure would climb.

By early Tuesday the Arakan Army and a senior local rescue official, Wai Hun Aung, said at least 49 people had died and 58 were injured, 22 of them critically. The market is the region's main wholesale hub, drawing traders from across the state. Images shared online showed burning buildings, wrecked vehicles and a collapsed section of a nearby bridge. The casualty figures could not be independently verified, and the military did not immediately respond; it has long said it strikes only legitimate targets and describes resistance groups as terrorists. Wai Hun Aung called it "one of the most severe airstrikes in Rakhine."

The attack fits a pattern of deadly air raids in areas the army has lost. Since launching an offensive in November 2023, the Arakan Army has taken a key regional military headquarters and 14 of Rakhine's 17 townships. The military has choked trade routes into the state, worsening food shortages, and in December an air strike on a hospital in Mrauk-U township killed more than 30 people.

Myanmar has been at war with itself since the army ousted Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in February 2021. Former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as president by a military-backed parliament in April. The UN says nearly half a million people are displaced in Rakhine, and the ACLED monitoring project estimates that more than 100,000 people have been killed nationwide.

The Arakan Army promised swift retaliation, raising the prospect of further fighting in the west of the country. Rights groups have repeatedly called for an arms and aviation-fuel embargo to curb the military's air campaign.
lead.why: Air strikes on civilian markets are among the deadliest features of Myanmar's civil war, which has displaced millions and destabilised a region bordering Bangladesh, India and China.

more.headline: AMD buys Fei-Fei Li's World Labs for $8.2 billion
more.dek: The chipmaker is acquiring the 'world model' start-up in an all-stock deal, with its founder becoming AMD's chief scientist.
body: AMD announced on 28 September that it will acquire World Labs, the AI start-up founded in 2024 by Stanford computer scientist Fei-Fei Li, for $8.2 billion. The deal, paid in AMD shares, is expected to close before the end of 2026 subject to regulatory approval. Li, best known for creating the ImageNet dataset, joins AMD as chief scientist reporting to chief executive Lisa Su.

World Labs builds 'world models' that try to understand physical space; its Marble product generates simulated 3D environments used in entertainment and to train robots. The price is roughly 75% above the company's valuation in a February funding round. Analysts see the purchase as a way for AMD to gain model-building credibility and compete with Nvidia, which already offers its own open world models.
more.why: The deal shows chipmakers moving up the AI stack into model research, and underlines the race to build simulation tools for robotics.

more.headline: Hurricane Polo slams into Mexico's Baja California peninsula
more.dek: Polo made landfall late on Monday in Baja California Sur before crossing the Gulf of California to hit Sonora and soak the US Southwest.
body: Hurricane Polo came ashore in Baja California Sur late on 28 September local time, near the middle of the peninsula in Comondú municipality, with sustained winds of around 110 mph (177 km/h). Hundreds of people took shelter, ports closed and the Mexican navy sent ships to help isolated coastal villages. The state governor reported mainly rain damage and no deaths or injuries.

The storm then crossed the Gulf of California and struck the Sonora coast near Guaymas on Tuesday as a weaker hurricane, flooding streets and knocking out power. Its remnants brought flash floods to Arizona, Utah and New Mexico, where some riverside communities were told to move to higher ground over fears of a dam failure, and flood watches stretched into the central US.
more.why: Polo was one of several strong storms in an active Eastern Pacific season, and its moisture caused flooding hundreds of miles inland in the United States.

lead.headline: Iran sends Hormuz reopening plan to Washington via Qatar
lead.dek: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Qatari mediators in New York and said he expected a US answer within a day, while Washington insisted any deal must cover Iran's nuclear programme.
body: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held talks with Qatari mediators in New York, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, about Tehran's plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Speaking to Iranian state media late on Monday, he said the Qataris would carry the ideas discussed to Washington and that Tehran hoped for a formal US reply by Tuesday. He described the exchange of messages through Qatari and Pakistani channels as having become more serious.

Iran's proposal, presented at the UN the previous Friday, asks the United States to unfreeze Iranian funds, lift sanctions and end its naval blockade of Iranian ports. Araghchi said those steps could be finished in four or five days, after which the strait would reopen, with talks on a final settlement, including the nuclear file, starting by day seven.

Washington's response was cool. President Donald Trump had called the plan "unacceptable" on Saturday. A US official described the indirect contacts as positive but said there would be no agreement to end the war without progress on Iran's nuclear programme, adding that the president was willing to ease sanctions and release funds in return. The official also accused Iran of breaching a June memorandum by firing on merchant ships; Tehran denies this and says the US failed to restrain Israeli attacks on Lebanon.

Iran shut the strait after the US and Israel launched their offensive on 28 February. Before the war, about a fifth of the world's oil and gas passed through it, and oil has since traded above $100 a barrel. Some tankers now use a US-escorted route along the Omani coast, and Gulf crude exports recovered to 12.8 million barrels a day in September, still well below February's level.

Iranian military leaders struck a defiant tone, saying the strait remains closed. The next test is whether Qatar can bridge the gap over sequencing: Iran wants economic relief first, while Washington wants nuclear commitments up front.
lead.why: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most important energy chokepoint, and its closure has kept oil and fuel prices high across the globe.

more.headline: US consumer confidence sinks to its lowest level since 2014
more.dek: The Conference Board's index fell to 81.9 in September as fuel prices and job worries weighed on households.
body: The Conference Board said on 29 September that its US consumer confidence index fell 6.7 points to 81.9, the weakest reading in about 12 years and far below the roughly 89 economists had expected. Its gauge of current conditions dropped to 109.3, and households' view of present business conditions turned negative for the first time since September 2024.

The expectations index slid to 63.6, its third straight fall and the 20th month in a row below 80, a level the group associates with recession risk. Written comments about prices, especially for oil and petrol, reached new highs, and more consumers expected interest rates to rise over the next year. One economist called the data a warning sign for holiday spending.
more.why: US consumers drive about two-thirds of the world's largest economy, so a slump in their mood can ripple through global trade and markets.

more.headline: Trump says top AI firms sign voluntary accord to police themselves
more.dek: Leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, Nvidia and xAI agreed at the White House to internal controls and outside audits.
body: After meeting AI executives at the White House on 29 September, President Trump announced a voluntary accord signed by the heads of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia and xAI and by OpenAI's president. The companies pledged to set up robust internal controls, hire independent auditors to test them, and create board committees to review the results, with a note that the steps might one day become law. Trump called the pact "morally binding" and said a small committee would oversee it.

Critics, including academics at USC and Harvard's Berkman Klein Center, said self-policing and vague wording are no substitute for legal liability and regulation. The announcement came a day after OpenAI said it was holding back a new model after internal safety tests, and on the same day it launched 'dots', an always-on personal AI agent.
more.why: With Washington refusing binding AI rules, voluntary pledges by a handful of US firms are effectively setting the guardrails for a technology used worldwide.

lead.headline: Last US troops leave Iraq, closing the anti-ISIS mission
lead.dek: American and coalition forces completed their departure from Erbil Air Base, ending Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq after 12 years.
body: US Central Command said on Wednesday 30 September that the last American troops and equipment had left Erbil Air Base in Iraq's Kurdistan region, completing the withdrawal of US and coalition forces from the country. The move ends Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, the campaign against the Islamic State group that began in 2014, under a transition plan Baghdad and Washington agreed in September 2024.

Erbil had been the main hub for the coalition task force and hosted most of the roughly 1,500 American and allied personnel still supporting counter-ISIS work. Most US forces left bases in federal Iraq last year. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell described an orderly departure, and CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said ISIS "no longer poses a systemic threat" to Iraq's security. President Trump called it a decisive victory.

US forces invaded Iraq in 2003, withdrew in 2011 and were invited back in 2014 after ISIS overran large parts of Iraq and Syria. Iraq declared territorial victory in 2017, but the coalition stayed to prevent a comeback. The task force has now moved its headquarters to Jordan and will keep fighting ISIS in Syria alongside partners and the Syrian government.

Reaction in Iraq was mixed. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi spoke of a new phase built on sovereignty, and an official of the Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah militia welcomed the exit. The Kurdish region's Peshmerga ministry, however, said leaving without providing an air-defence system was worrying, noting the region had faced more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks during the recent US-Iran conflict.

Relations will now shift to a conventional bilateral defence partnership, with Washington offering training and intelligence. Iraqi forces take primary responsibility for remaining ISIS cells and for the Iran-backed militias that analysts expect to test the new arrangement.
lead.why: The exit ends more than two decades of near-continuous US military involvement in Iraq at a time when the wider region is gripped by the US-Iran war.

more.headline: China threatens firm response if EU builds new anti-China trade tool
more.dek: Beijing's commerce ministry warned Brussels against a proposed 'European 301' instrument modelled on US trade law.
body: China's Ministry of Commerce said late on 29 September that it would "respond firmly" if the European Union adopted new restrictions on Chinese companies or goods. It called a proposed EU trade instrument, modelled on the US Section 301 law against unfair trade practices, protectionist and unilateral, and warned that adding pressure while talks were under way would damage trust.

The warning followed reports that several member states, reportedly led by Germany and France, were preparing a joint paper urging the European Commission to speed up the tool. Chinese state media said Beijing had a 'strong policy toolbox' to hit back, including anti-discrimination probes and supply-chain security reviews. The two sides are currently in trade and investment consultations covering imbalances, export controls and intellectual property.
more.why: A new EU-China trade fight would hit the world's second- and third-largest economies and add strain to global supply chains already stressed by the Gulf war.

more.headline: Boeing wins US Navy's $20 billion next-generation fighter contract
more.dek: The F/A-XX award gives Boeing both of America's sixth-generation fighter programmes.
body: The US Navy awarded Boeing a development contract worth about $20 billion for its F/A-XX carrier-based sixth-generation fighter, announced late on 29 September. Northrop Grumman had competed for the work. The aircraft will eventually replace the F/A-18 Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler and fly alongside F-35Cs and combat drones. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao called it a generational leap in air superiority.

Boeing already won the Air Force's F-47 programme in March 2025, and will build both jets mainly in St. Louis. Congress revived F/A-XX after the Pentagon had tried to slow it to prioritise the F-47. Boeing shares rose about 3% on the news, and some analysts suggest the new jet could fly before the end of the decade.
more.why: The contract shapes how the US Navy will project power from aircraft carriers for decades and reshapes the competitive landscape of the global defence industry.

lead.headline: Russian drones hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge, halting metro across Dnipro
lead.dek: Two drones struck near the supports of the cable-stayed bridge, the first drone attack on one of the capital's river crossings.
body: Two Russian drones hit the Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge in Kyiv at around 11:30 local time on Thursday 1 October, while cars and a metro train were crossing. Footage showed an explosion near one of the columns of the cable-stayed bridge and thick black smoke rising from the structure, which carries road traffic and metro trains between the city's eastern and western banks.

Mayor Vitali Klitschko said metro and surface public transport over the bridge had been halted while engineers inspected it, and that it was the first time drones had targeted one of the capital's bridges. Dust entered the passing train through its vents, but no passengers were hurt. Traffic resumed by mid-afternoon after a preliminary check found no critical structural damage. The same night, drones hit a school in Solomianskyi district, where pupils were sheltering, and destroyed a data centre at a Pecherskyi exhibition complex.

The strike followed a warning a day earlier from Sergiy Beskrestnov, a presidential adviser, that Russia had begun using a new jet-powered drone designed to cut power pylons and steel bridge structures. Jet drones are faster and harder to shoot down than the older Shahed-type models. Ukraine's air force counted 3,177 Russian drone strikes up to 29 September, up from 2,850 in August, and Kyiv says Moscow has begun a campaign to knock out power and heating before winter.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia must be held fully accountable and must face a response. Elsewhere in Ukraine, overnight attacks killed at least six people and injured 38.
Kyiv's roughly three million residents depend on the Dnipro bridges, and officials fear further attacks. Within days, Russian drones also struck the city's Northern Bridge.
lead.why: Attacks on Kyiv's river crossings and energy grid signal a new phase of Russia's air campaign aimed at paralysing Ukraine's capital ahead of winter.

more.headline: Swiss glaciers lose more than 5% of their ice in a year
more.dek: Monitors say 2026 was the second-worst melt year on record, with several small glaciers vanishing entirely.
body: Switzerland's glaciers lost about 5.5% of their remaining ice in 2026, according to the annual report from the GLAMOS monitoring network and the Swiss Academy of Sciences. That is just short of the record 6% loss in 2022. Allalin, Clariden, Aletsch and Rhône glaciers had their greatest melt ever, and small ice fields such as Bella Tola disappeared. Swiss ice volume has fallen by almost a fifth in five years.

A dry winter left little protective snow, and the freezing level sat above 4,000 metres on a record 76 days between May and September. Glaciologist Matthias Huss described one site as "a moon landscape that is dry and dead." Low river levels this summer disrupted Rhine and Danube shipping, and scientists project Swiss glaciers could vanish by 2100 on current warming.
more.why: Alpine glaciers act as Europe's water towers, feeding rivers used for drinking water, farming, shipping and power-plant cooling.

more.headline: Klopp earns first Germany win as Portugal cope without Ronaldo
more.dek: Germany beat Serbia 2-0 in Munich, while Portugal won 4-2 in Denmark a day after Cristiano Ronaldo left the squad.
body: Jürgen Klopp recorded his first win as Germany coach at the third attempt, a 2-0 Nations League victory over Serbia in Munich on 1 October. Tom Bischof scored his first senior international goal after Florian Wirtz hit the post, and Wirtz added the second after the hour. Klopp had opened with a draw against the Netherlands and a defeat to Greece, and fielded an entirely changed starting line-up including two debutants.

In Copenhagen, Portugal beat Denmark 4-2 in their first game since Ronaldo walked out following an apparent rift with coach Jorge Jesus. João Cancelo, Vitinha and João Félix were among the scorers as Portugal stayed top of their group with maximum points.
more.why: Germany's revival under one of football's best-known coaches and Ronaldo's uncertain international future are two of European football's biggest storylines.

lead.headline: US hiring nearly stalls with just 29,000 jobs in September
lead.dek: Payroll growth missed forecasts, earlier months were revised down by 60,000 and unemployment rose to 4.2%.
body: US employers added only 29,000 jobs in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday 2 October, well below the roughly 90,000 economists expected and under the 45,000 monthly average of the past year. The unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% from 4.1%, leaving 7.1 million people out of work. The rate has stayed between 4.1% and 4.3% since March.

Revisions made the picture weaker. July's figure was cut from a gain of 21,000 to a loss of 10,000, and August's from 162,000 to 133,000, removing 60,000 jobs in total. Health care added 17,000 jobs, construction 11,000 and manufacturing 9,000, while government shed 17,000, information 10,000 and financial activities 7,000.

Pay growth slowed. Average hourly earnings rose just 5 cents to $37.81, up 3.0% from a year earlier, which analysts at First Trust noted is lagging consumer price inflation. The household survey was firmer: participation rose to 61.8% and the labour force grew by nearly half a million people, suggesting the job market is cooling rather than collapsing.

The report lands as the US economy absorbs high fuel prices driven by the war with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and days after consumer confidence fell to its lowest since 2014. Federal government jobs have dropped sharply over the past year, while factory and construction hiring has been supported by data-centre building.

For the Federal Reserve, which raised rates in September, the soft numbers make another hike at its October meeting less likely, according to First Trust, pushing the debate towards December. The next jobs report is due in early November, just after the midterm elections.
lead.why: The US labour market underpins global demand, and a stalling job engine could tip the world's largest economy towards recession while inflation stays high.

more.headline: G7 agrees to release up to 100 million barrels of oil
more.dek: Leaders backed a four-month release of emergency reserves, front-loaded with diesel, to calm record fuel prices.
body: G7 countries agreed on 2 October to release up to 100 million barrels of strategic oil reserves over four months, coordinated through the International Energy Agency, after a call chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron. The plan includes a large diesel release within the first 20 days, coordinated refinery maintenance and a pledge to avoid energy export restrictions between G7 members.

Diesel prices have hit records on both sides of the Atlantic: the UK average passed £2 a litre for the first time, and the US average reached $6.37 a gallon. Donald Trump, who had floated banning US diesel exports unless Europe released its stocks, claimed credit for the deal. The IEA's 32 members had already agreed a 400-million-barrel release in March.
more.why: Coordinated stock releases are the main tool rich countries have to cushion households from the oil shock caused by the Gulf war.

more.headline: Meta opens its Muse AI agent to home-built gadgets
more.dek: New open-source code lets hobbyists run Meta's personal AI agent on cheap boards such as the ESP32 and Raspberry Pi.
body: Meta released open-source code on 2 October that lets developers build their own hardware for Muse, the personal AI agent it launched in September. The SDK runs on ESP32 microcontroller boards and small Linux computers, so builders can attach screens, buttons, sensors and other devices, from colour e-ink notification panels to tiny touchscreen 'charms'. Meta also announced Muse Home Link, a USB adapter free to US subscribers that lets the agent reach devices on a home network.

Meta warns builders to proceed at their own risk, and reviewers note that although the code is open, Meta controls the access tokens needed to use it and can revoke them. The move came days after OpenAI launched its rival 'dots' agents.
more.why: Big Tech's race to put AI agents into everyday objects is moving from phones to homes, raising questions about control and privacy.

lead.headline: UAE calls FlyDubai cockpit axe attack an act of terrorism
lead.dek: A co-pilot struck the captain with the crash axe on a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight; passengers subdued him and the jet landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
body: The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, said a FlyDubai co-pilot attacked his captain with the cockpit's crash axe and tried to take control of the aircraft on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. UAE Prosecutor General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said the co-pilot had attempted a terrorist act. The incident took place on Wednesday 30 September; the UAE gave details on 3 October.

The plane, carrying 182 people, most of them Israeli, plunged roughly 17,000 feet, steeply enough that part of the rudder was torn away. The captain, Indian pilot Smit Machchhar, was badly wounded but managed to unlock the cockpit door. Passengers and off-duty crew overpowered the co-pilot, and two other pilots on board stabilised the jet, which made an emergency landing in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the attacker and handed him to the UAE.

People familiar with the case identified the co-pilot as Hamam al-Hammami, a UAE-born Omani national. Oman Air had reportedly grounded him over concerns about extremist views before FlyDubai hired him; a Gulf diplomat said he passed standard checks. Officials had not formally confirmed his identity. Investigators from four regional states, helped by the US and others, have so far found no links to militant groups.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel was examining whether anyone directed the attack and praised the captain for saving many lives. FlyDubai suspended its Israel route and El Al cancelled flights, stranding some travellers until repatriation flights began. Questions remain over how a pilot from a country without ties to Israel was rostered on the route.
The case has prompted calls to tighten cross-border background checks on pilots, which vary widely between countries.
lead.why: An attack from inside the cockpit exposes gaps in airline crew vetting worldwide and strains fragile Israel-Gulf air links.

more.headline: Huge crowds march across Spain over housing crisis
more.dek: Protests in Madrid and about 50 other cities followed parliament's rejection of two tenant-protection decrees.
body: Tens of thousands of people demonstrated in Madrid and some 50 other Spanish cities on 3 October, a day after Congress voted down two government decrees meant to protect renters. Organisers put the Madrid crowd at 500,000; authorities said about 70,000. In Valencia, police fired rubber bullets and tear gas at protesters marching on a property investment conference. The Tenants' Union is calling for a 50% rent cut and a general strike.

The movement grew after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her Madrid home of seven decades, prompting a protest camp in Puerta del Sol. The decrees failed after Catalan party Junts joined the conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox against them, and opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo demanded early elections.
more.why: Spain's revolt over rents reflects a housing affordability crisis felt in cities across Europe and beyond.

more.headline: Latvian PM's United List wins big in security-focused election
more.dek: Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centre-right party took about 35% of the vote, while a party critics call pro-Russian came third.
body: Latvians voted on 3 October in a parliamentary election dominated by fears of Russia, living costs and strained health care. Preliminary results showed Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' United List with about 35% and a projected 42 of the 100 seats, its best result since independence. Latvia First, led by a populist property magnate, came second, and Sovereign Power, which opposes military aid to Ukraine, came third. Turnout was about 52%.

Kulbergs, in office since May, said voters wanted change, but one of his coalition partners, the Union of Greens and Farmers, fell just short of the 5% threshold, so he must find new allies. Most mainstream parties have ruled out working with Sovereign Power. Official results are due by 19 October.
more.why: Latvia sits on NATO's eastern flank, and its politics on defence and Ukraine are closely watched as Russia steps up pressure on Europe.

lead.headline: Brazil heads to Lula-Bolsonaro runoff as the right surges
lead.dek: Senator Flávio Bolsonaro took about 47% to President Lula's 45% in the first round, setting up a 25 October runoff.
body: Brazil's presidential election will be decided in a runoff on 25 October after neither candidate passed 50% of valid votes on Sunday 4 October. With nearly all ballots counted, right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro had about 47%, roughly 56 million votes, against about 45% for left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Most pre-election polls had shown Lula finishing first, so the result surprised analysts.

Bolsonaro, 45, is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who lost narrowly to Lula in 2022 and is now serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting to overturn that result. Flávio has promised to continue his father's legacy, cut the deficit and realign foreign policy with Washington. He declared the vote "the end of the Workers' Party era." Lula, 80 and seeking a fourth term, said a new campaign begins now and that he thrives in knockout rounds.

The right also did well in Congress. Bolsonaro's Liberal Party was on course to become the largest party in the lower house and gained Senate seats; Michelle Bolsonaro won a Senate seat in the Federal District, and Carlos Bolsonaro was elected senator in Santa Catarina. Third- to fifth-placed presidential candidates were all on the right, although two of them, Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, said they would not endorse anyone.

The United States looms over the race. Donald Trump's administration is pushing to shift Latin America rightward; Lula has accused Washington of meddling, which the State Department denies, and has campaigned on protecting Brazil's sovereignty. Voters say security, corruption and the economy are their top concerns.

Lula must now rebuild the broad coalition that elected him in 2022, including less enthusiastic young voters, in a three-week sprint. Observers will also watch for a repeat of the political violence that marked the last runoff.
lead.why: Brazil is Latin America's largest economy and democracy, and the runoff will decide whether it stays on a left-leaning, independent course or aligns with Trump's Washington.

more.headline: Merz brings €1.3 billion aid package to Kyiv amid bridge strikes
more.dek: Germany's chancellor pledged military and energy aid as Russian drones hit another Kyiv bridge during his visit.
body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a visit to Kyiv on 4 October and announced more than €1.3 billion in new support: about €1 billion in military aid, including long-range weapons, combat drones and satellite technology, and €350 million to repair the energy grid before winter. German firms signed defence deals with Ukraine covering IRIS-T air-defence missiles, radar and jet-drone interceptors; Reuters put 14 deals at about €6.6 billion, while Zelensky cited 15 agreements worth more than €8.5 billion.

During the visit, a Russian drone struck Kyiv's Northern Bridge, wounding two people; three of the city's six road bridges have been fully or partly closed since Thursday. Merz said Germany "will not be intimidated" and urged Vladimir Putin to end the war. The US has proposed technical-level three-way talks by late October.
more.why: Germany is Ukraine's biggest European backer, and its aid is central to Kyiv's ability to defend cities and power plants from Russia's escalating drone war.

more.headline: Djokovic fights back to beat top seed Zverev in Beijing
more.dek: The 39-year-old came from a set down to reach the China Open semi-finals, where he faces Daniil Medvedev.
body: Novak Djokovic beat top seed Alexander Zverev 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 in the China Open quarter-finals in Beijing on 4 October, in a match lasting about two hours and 35 minutes. After a slow start in cold conditions, the Serb broke serve late in each of the last two sets to win. Zverev, the reigning French Open and US Open champion, served 19 aces.

Djokovic, a six-time champion in Beijing who has never lost a match there, is playing the event for the first time since 2015 and is chasing his first title of 2026. He said the win showed he could still beat the best on big stages. He next meets Daniil Medvedev, who beat Francisco Cerundolo 7-6, 6-3.
more.why: Djokovic's late-career run against the sport's new leaders keeps one of tennis's greatest players in the title hunt.
